translations.source_sense_description: Einrichtungsgegenstand in der Küche zum Reinigen

glosses: To move or be moved into something.
To descend or submerge (or to cause to do so) into a liquid or similar substance.

examples.text: A stone sinks in water.  The sun gradually sank in the west.

glosses: To move or be moved into something.
To (directly or indirectly) cause a vessel to sink, generally by making it no longer watertight.

examples.text: An iceberg sank the Titanic.  British battleships sank the Bismarck.

glosses: To move or be moved into something.
To push (something) into something.

examples.text: Before installing the new surfacing material, sink any protruding nails.
The joint will hold tighter if you sink a wood screw through both boards.  The dog sank its teeth into the delivery man's leg.

glosses: To move or be moved into something.
To make by digging or delving.

examples.text: to sink a well in the ground

glosses: To move or be moved into something.
To pot; hit a ball into a pocket or hole.

examples.text: My sister beats me at pool in public a second time. I claim some dignity back by potting two of my balls before Tammy sinks the black.

glosses: To diminish or be diminished.
To experience apprehension, disappointment, dread, or momentary depression.

examples.text:
But open converse is there none,
⁠So much the vital spirits sink
⁠To see the vacant chair, and think,
‘How good! how kind! and he is gone.’

I tried, but I could not wake him. This caused me a great fear, and I looked around terrified. Then indeed, my heart sank within me. Beside the bed, as if he had stepped out of the mist, or rather as if the mist had turned into his figure, for it had entirely disappeared, stood a tall, thin man, all in black.
Peter's heart sank. "Don't you think it is dreadful?" he asked.

glosses: To diminish or be diminished.
To cause to decline; to depress or degrade.

examples.text: to sink one's reputation
And if I have a conscience, let it sink me
Thy cruel and unnatural lust of power / Has sunk thy father more than all his years.

glosses: To diminish or be diminished.
To demean or lower oneself; to do something below one's status, standards, or morals.

examples.text: Who would sink so low as to steal change from veterans?

glosses: To conceal and appropriate.

examples.text: If you are sent with ready money to buy anything at a shop, and happen at that time to be out of pocket, sink the money, and take up the goods on your master's account.

glosses: To keep out of sight; to suppress; to ignore.

examples.text: I say not always dishonorable qualifications, but a certain flexibility of disposition; a certain courtly willingness to sink obnoxious truths, and adapt ourselves to the prejudices of the minds of others […]

glosses: To drink (especially something alcoholic).

examples.text: […] just thought she was wrecked from all the Diamond White ciders she'd been sinking – I'd even bought her a couple of Blastaways, which in hindsight was a mistake.

glosses: To pay absolutely.

examples.text: I have sunk thousands of pounds into this project.
for 13 of his 15 years in charge, Burrell sank more money into the farm than he received in revenues, and the estate was £1.5m overdrawn.

glosses: To reduce or extinguish by payment.

examples.text: to sink the national debt

glosses: To be overwhelmed or depressed; to fail in strength.

examples.text: I think our country sinks beneath the yoke.
then keep an even steady Fire under them, not too fierce at first, lest you scorch them; and let not the Fire sink or slacken, but rather increase till the Hops be near dry'd

glosses: To die.

examples.text: However, before the entire mass was detached, a copious oozing of blood took place, when the patient lost from a pint to a pint and a half; and which, doubtless, so lowered him that he never rallied, but sank in about an hour and a half after the operation was completed.

[…] as September drew towards its close, and reports came from Munich that Gömbös was sinking fast, the Right in their turn were credited by the Prager Presse and by certain foreign journalists, who drew their inspiration from the same sources, with sensational designs.

glosses: To decrease in volume, as a river; to subside; to become diminished in volume or in apparent height.

examples.text: The Alps and Pyreneans sink before him: / Through wind and waves, and storms he works his way

It was not far from the house; but the ground sank into a depression there, and the ridge of it behind shut out everything except just the roof of the tallest hayrick. As one sat on the sward behind the elm, with the back turned on the rick and nothing in front but the tall elms and the oaks in the other hedge, it was quite easy to fancy it the verge of the prairie with the backwoods close by.

glosses: A basin used for holding water for washing.

examples.text:
Roy: The work was fiiine. There was nothing wrong with the work. But they caught him... He pissed in the sink.
Jen: Oh. Oh!
Roy: Yeah...
Jen: Which sink?
Roy: All the sinks. Yeah, he basically went on a pee parade around the house.
Jen: Oh God, I have to fire him.

glosses: A drain for carrying off wastewater.
A sinkhole.
A depression in land where water collects, with no visible outlet.
A heat sink.
A place that absorbs resources or energy.
A habitat that cannot support a population on its own but receives the excess of individuals from some other source.
Descending motion; descent.

examples.text: An excessive sink rate at touchdown can cause the aircraft's landing gear to collapse.

glosses: Descending motion; descent.
The motion of a sinker pitch.

examples.text: Jones has a two-seamer with heavy sink.

glosses: An object or callback that captures events.
A destination vertex in a transportation network.
A node in directed graph for which all of its edges go into it; one with no outgoing edges.
An abode of degraded persons; a wretched place.
A depression in a stereotype plate.
A stage trapdoor for shifting scenery.
An excavation smaller than a shaft.
One or several systems that remove currency from the game's economy, thus controlling or preventing inflation.
